title: Expected Value
short: The long-run average outcome: Σ x · P(x).
trouble: Students think the expected value must be a value the variable can take.

blocks.html: A probability distribution lists every value and its chance. One number summarizes where it is centered: the expected value, the long-run average of the variable over many repetitions.

The expected value (mean) of a discrete random variable is $$\role[expected value]{integral}{E(X)} = \mu = \sum \role[value]{input}{x} \cdot \role[probability of that value]{probability}{P(x)},$$ each value weighted by its probability. It is the average you would see in the long run, and it does not have to be a possible value of $X$.

Imagine repeating the process $N$ times, with $N$ large. The value $x$ shows up about $N \cdot P(x)$ times, so the total of all results is about $\sum x \cdot N P(x)$. Divide by $N$ to get the average: $\sum x P(x)$. It is the same as a mean computed from a frequency table, with probabilities in place of relative frequencies.

blocks.title: One die
blocks.q: Find the expected value of one roll of a fair die.
steps: Each value from 1 to 6 has probability $\frac{1}{6}$.
No roll ever shows 3.5. It is the long-run average of many rolls.

blocks.title: A game
blocks.q: A game costs \$2. You win \$10 with probability $0.1$, \$3 with probability $0.2$, and nothing otherwise. What is the expected net gain per game?
steps: On average you lose 40 cents per game; over 100 games, about \$40.

blocks.name: dice
blocks.cap: Roll one die many times. The bars level out at 1/6 each, and the long-run average of the rolls settles near 3.5.

blocks.html: Thinking the expected value must be a value the variable can take, or the most likely value. The expected number of pets is 1.4, though no household has 1.4 pets. Check: E(X) is an average, a balance point, not a prediction for one trial.
